passages.t: Four chariots go out over the earth
passages.happening: Zechariah sees four chariots coming out from between two mountains of bronze (verse 1). The first has red horses, the second black, the third white and the fourth dappled, all of them strong (verses 2-3). The angel tells him, ‘These are the four spirits of heaven, going forth from their station before the Lord of all the earth’ (verse 5). The black horses go toward the land of the north, the white toward the west, the dappled toward the south (verse 6). They are eager to go, and the LORD sends them to patrol the earth (verse 7). Then he says that those going to the north have given rest to his Spirit in the land of the north (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
This is the eighth and last vision. It matches the first: horses patrolling the earth. In the first vision the earth was at rest while Jerusalem lay in ruins. Now God's chariots go out, and his Spirit is at rest in the north.

The land of the north means Babylon and the lands beyond it, from which invaders had always come into Israel and where many exiles still lived. The four chariots, like the four horns of chapter 1, point to the four directions and so to the whole earth; the word for the four spirits can also mean the four winds.
passages.later: The first vision also showed horses that ‘patrol the earth’ (Zechariah 1:10). Jeremiah had warned that disaster would come ‘from the north’ (Jeremiah 1:14).
passages.asks: God's chariots go out over the whole earth. Ask what it means to you that no part of the world is outside God's rule. And ask where you need God's Spirit to be at rest.

passages.t: A crown for Joshua, and the man called the Branch
passages.happening:
God tells Zechariah to take silver and gold from exiles newly come from Babylon, Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah, and go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah (verses 9-10). ‘Take silver and gold, make an ornate crown, and set it on the head of the high priest, Joshua son of Jehozadak’ (verse 11).

He is to say that the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Here is a man whose name is the Branch, and He will branch out from His place and build the temple of the LORD’ (verse 12). He will be clothed in splendor and sit on his throne and rule, ‘And He will be a priest on His throne, and there will be peaceful counsel between the two’ (verse 13). The crown will be kept in the temple as a memorial (verse 14). Even those far away will come and help build the temple, if the people carefully obey the LORD (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is a sign act, not a vision. Zechariah uses gifts brought by exiles to make a crown and set it on the high priest's head. The crown is then laid up in the temple to remember the promise.

The Branch is a title for a king from David's line. Here the Branch will build the temple, rule on a throne and be a priest on a throne, joining roles that Israel kept apart. Peaceful counsel between the two may mean harmony between the royal and priestly offices.

The promise of verse 15, those far away will come and build, depends on obedience. The book holds the promise and the condition together.
passages.later: A psalm speaks of a king who is also ‘a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek’ (Psalm 110:4). Ezra tells of gifts brought by returning exiles for the house of God (Ezra 2:68-69).
passages.hard:
Why is the crown placed on Joshua the priest rather than on Zerubbabel, the heir of David?

Several explanations are offered. Some scholars propose that the original text named Zerubbabel and was later changed to Joshua when Zerubbabel disappeared from history without becoming king; this is a conjecture without manuscript support. Others suggest that the plural crowns in verse 11 point to two crowns, one for each leader, though the text mentions only Joshua. Many interpreters hold that the text means what it says: Joshua is crowned as a sign, not as king. The words are spoken to him but speak of another, a man whose name is the Branch, and the crown is then laid up in the temple for that coming one. These notes leave the explanations open.
passages.asks: The crown was laid up in the temple as a memorial of a promise. Ask what promise of God you need to keep in front of you. And ask what it would mean to obey carefully while you wait for it.
